Keeping your place is a separate job from reading

A fixture. Every element below is here to catch a specific mistake.

A page of unbroken prose asks the reader to do two things at once. The first is the one they came for: turning marks into words, words into sentences, and sentences into an argument they can hold in their head while the next sentence arrives. The second is bookkeeping — where am I, which line was I on, have I read this bit already or does it only feel familiar because the sentence before it ended the same way. The second job is invisible until it fails.

When it fails it fails silently. The eye reaches the right-hand margin, drops, and sweeps back left across an inch of undifferentiated grey with nothing at the far end to aim at. Most of the time it lands correctly. When it doesn't, a line gets read twice, or skipped, and the argument being held in working memory slips. Rebuilding it costs real effort. After four or five repetitions the reader closes the tab, and an abandoned article is read at no words per minute at all.

This paragraph exists to be found. Search this page for the phrase undifferentiated grey with nothing and the browser should highlight it, even though Gradient Reader has by then cut that phrase into eight separate elements. If find-in-page cannot match across those boundaries the whole approach is dead, which is why it is the first thing to check and not the last.

Large speed gains without comprehension loss are overstated, and these tools typically alter visual functions that are hard constraints or actively useful.1

The claim being made here is narrow on purpose. Colour continuity across the return sweep may help a reader keep their place, so they fall off long text less often. It does not make anybody read faster: gaze-contingent work puts the useful window of word availability at fifty or sixty milliseconds, and the rest of the time goes on language processing that no rendering treatment touches. The speed claim is the one thing in this category that has been actively disproven, and not making it is the difference between a product that ages well and one that doesn't.

Some inline oddities, all of which must survive: a superscript2 mid-sentence, a piece of inline_code_untouched() which must keep its own font and colour, an emphasis inside a strong inside emphasis, and a phrase the site paints with background-clip which must not swallow the gradient.

Emoji and combining characters are here because chunking splits text every few characters, and splitting one of these in half does not merely look wrong, it produces a different character: a café in Zürich 👍🏽, a family 👨‍👩‍👧, a flag 🇮🇳, and the word नमस्ते.

Things that must be left completely alone

Each of the next four blocks is on the never-touch list. If any of them picks up a colour, that is a bug in detect.js.

function paint(spans, layout) {
  //   whitespace and alignment carry meaning in here
  for (const span of spans) span.style.color = next();
}

One last paragraph of ordinary prose, so that the end of the article is somewhere plain rather than in the middle of a test case. There is nothing special about this one at all, which is itself the point: most of a page is this, and most of a page is what has to come out right.

How to use this file

  1. Turn it on. Click the Gradient Reader icon, then Turn on for this page. Prose should colour; nav, the headline, pre, the table, the form, the editable box and the maths should not.
  2. Find in page. Ctrl+F or Cmd+F, search undifferentiated grey with nothing. It must match and highlight. This is the check that decides whether the approach works at all.
  3. Copy and paste. Select the first two paragraphs, copy, paste into a plain text editor. No stray spaces, no missing spaces, no fragments.
  4. Screen reader. With VoiceOver or NVDA, read the first paragraph. It must say whole words. If it reads "undiff" "erent" "iated", stop — spans are reaching the accessibility tree and that has to be fixed before anything else.
  5. Links. The word disproven above is a link. With the gradient on it loses its blue, so it must have gained an underline.
  6. Zoom. Ctrl+plus a few times. Lines break in new places, so the colour must re-flow to match — and it must do it by re-measuring, not by re-wrapping. Watch for a stall.
  7. Turn it off. The page must return to exactly how it started: no leftover colour, no leftover spans, nav and form untouched.
  8. Console. One line from Gradient Reader saying how many blocks, lines and spans, and the first-paint time. Nothing else, and no errors.
